## Introduction

This tutorial covers [Chapter 15: Applications: Foundations](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/foundations-applications.html) from [*Introduction to Modern Statistics*](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/) by Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel and Johanna Hardin. You will learn to judge whether a difference between two groups in a small randomized experiment could be due to chance alone, by simulating the experiment's random assignment many times, and to tell apart the data, randomization, and bootstrap distributions.

### Exercise 1

You should be doing this tutorial in a repo named `applications-foundations`. If you are not, create one and then connect to it.

Create a new file, `analysis.qmd`, with the title `"Applications: Foundations"` and your name as the author. In a bash Terminal, render it:

```bash
quarto render analysis.qmd
```

Open `analysis.html` with Live Server (right-click it in the Explorer → **Open with Live Server**) and keep the tab open. It refreshes on every render. Going forward, we will just tell you to "Render" when we want you to take these steps.

Create a `.gitignore` with `analysis_files` followed by a blank line. Commit and push. Use AI however you like.

If `show_file()` fails, it is probably because you have not yet loaded `library(learnr2)` in the R Terminal.

```{r}
#| label: introduction-1
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file(".gitignore"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{.output}
analysis_files
```

###

In the foundations of inference chapters, we have provided three different methods for statistical inference: randomization, bootstrapping, and mathematical models. This chapter applies the first of them to a single small experiment.

## Variability within data

In this case study, we consider a new malaria vaccine called PfSPZ. This section looks at the data from its 20 volunteers.

### Exercise 1

Add a chunk that prints `malaria`. Render.

```{r}
#| label: variability-within-data-1
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: variability-within-data-1-test
#| echo: true
malaria
```

###

Each of the 20 rows is one volunteer. Nineteen weeks after vaccination, all 20 patients were exposed to a drug-sensitive strain of the malaria parasite, allowing any infections to be treated effectively.

### Exercise 2

Replace the code in that chunk so that it counts the volunteers in each `treatment` group. Render.

```{r}
#| label: variability-within-data-2
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: variability-within-data-2-test
#| echo: true
malaria |>
  count(treatment)
```

###

The study is an experiment, as patients were randomly assigned an experiment group: 14 to the vaccine and 6 to a placebo. The patients were volunteers, not a random sample, so its conclusions are cause and effect but might not generalize because of volunteer bias.

![](images/fig-randsampValloc.png){fig-alt="A two by two table describing the scenarios of random sample or not and random allocation or not. Selecting randomly from a population allows for generalization back to the population. Randomly allocating in an experiment allows for establishing causation."}

### Exercise 3

Replace the code in that chunk so that it counts the volunteers by both `treatment` and `outcome`. Render.

```{r}
#| label: variability-within-data-3
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: variability-within-data-3-test
#| echo: true
malaria |>
  count(treatment, outcome)
```

###

Two treatments and two outcomes make four combinations, but the count shows only three. The missing one, placebo with no infection, has no volunteers, and `count()` lists only combinations that occur.

### Exercise 4

Change the code so that the count also shows combinations with no volunteers in them. Render.

```{r}
#| label: variability-within-data-4

learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: variability-within-data-4-test
#| echo: true
malaria |>
  count(treatment, outcome, .drop = FALSE)
```

###

The zero is now a row of its own: placebo, no infection, 0. Dropping it would hide the study's most striking fact.

### Exercise 5

Reshape that count into a two-way table, with one row for each `treatment` and one column for each `outcome`. Render.

```{r}
#| label: variability-within-data-5
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: variability-within-data-5-test
#| echo: true
malaria |>
  count(treatment, outcome, .drop = FALSE) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = outcome, values_from = n)
```

###

This is the chapter's summary table: 9 of the 14 treatment patients remained free of signs of infection while all of the 6 patients in the control group showed some baseline signs of infection.

### Exercise 6

Replace the code in that chunk so that it calculates, for each `treatment` group, the number of volunteers and the proportion who got an infection. Render.

```{r}
#| label: variability-within-data-6
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: variability-within-data-6-test
#| echo: true
malaria |>
  summarize(n = n(),
            infection_rate = mean(outcome == "infection"),
            .by = treatment)
```

###

In this study, a smaller proportion of patients who received the vaccine showed signs of an infection (35.7% versus 100%). However, the sample is very small, and it is unclear whether the difference provides *convincing evidence* that the vaccine is effective.

### Exercise 7

Replace the code in that chunk so that it calculates a single number: the infection rate in the placebo group minus the infection rate in the vaccine group. Use **infer**. Render.

```{r}
#| label: variability-within-data-7
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: variability-within-data-7-test
#| echo: true
malaria |>
  specify(response = outcome, explanatory = treatment, success = "infection") |>
  calculate(stat = "diff in props", order = c("placebo", "vaccine"))
```

###

The observed difference is 0.643, or 64.3 percentage points. Under the *independence model*, $H_0$, the variables are independent and this difference was due to chance, while under the *alternative model*, $H_A$, it was not due to chance.

### Exercise 8

Replace the code in that chunk with a bar plot of the data: one bar for each `treatment` group, filled by `outcome`, with each bar showing proportions rather than counts. Render.

```{r}
#| label: variability-within-data-8
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: variability-within-data-8-test
#| echo: true
malaria |>
  ggplot(aes(x = treatment, fill = outcome)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill")
```

###

This plot shows the *data distribution*, which describes the shape, center, and variability of the observed data. Bars of equal height hide the fact that the placebo bar stands for 6 people and the vaccine bar for 14.

### Exercise 9

Improve the plot. Show the y-axis as percentages, move the legend below the plot, and add a title, axis labels, a subtitle that states the main finding, and a caption giving the number of volunteers in each group and the source. Render.

```{r}
#| label: variability-within-data-9
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: variability-within-data-9-test
#| echo: true
malaria |>
  ggplot(aes(x = treatment, fill = outcome)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  labs(title = "Infections in the PfSPZ Malaria Vaccine Trial",
       subtitle = "36% of vaccinated volunteers showed signs of infection, against all six given the placebo",
       x = "Treatment",
       y = "Percent of Volunteers",
       fill = "Outcome",
       caption = "20 volunteers: 14 vaccine, 6 placebo; Lyke et al. (2017), via openintro") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

###

The observed infection rates (35.7% for the treatment group versus 100% for the control group) suggest the vaccine may be effective. But with such small samples, perhaps it's common to observe such large differences when we randomly split a group due to chance alone.

This example is a reminder that the observed outcomes in the data sample may not perfectly reflect the true relationships between variables since there is *random noise*. The next section measures how much noise a study of 20 people can produce.

## Simulating the study

We're going to implement *simulation* under the setting where we will pretend we know that the malaria vaccine being tested does *not* work. Then 11 patients were going to develop an infection *no matter which group they were randomized into*. Ultimately, we want to understand if the large difference we observed in the data is common in these simulations that represent independence.

### Exercise 1

Start a new chunk that simulates one re-randomization under the independence model: keep each volunteer's outcome, but shuffle which 14 got the vaccine and which 6 got the placebo. Count the volunteers in the shuffled data by `treatment` and `outcome`, keeping empty combinations. Set a seed first, so the render gives the same shuffle every time. Render.

```{r}
#| label: simulating-the-study-1
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: simulating-the-study-1-test
#| echo: true
set.seed(15)
malaria |>
  specify(response = outcome, explanatory = treatment, success = "infection") |>
  hypothesize(null = "independence") |>
  generate(reps = 1, type = "permute") |>
  count(treatment, outcome, .drop = FALSE)
```

###

Your shuffle may differ from ours, but the totals cannot: 14 vaccine, 6 placebo, 11 infections, 9 without. By hand, we would write down "infection" on 11 cards and "no infection" on 9 cards, thoroughly shuffle the notecards, and deal 14 into a pile and 6 into a pile.

### Exercise 2

Replace the count with the difference in infection rates, placebo minus vaccine, for that one shuffle. Render.

```{r}
#| label: simulating-the-study-2
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: simulating-the-study-2-test
#| echo: true
set.seed(15)
malaria |>
  specify(response = outcome, explanatory = treatment, success = "infection") |>
  hypothesize(null = "independence") |>
  generate(reps = 1, type = "permute") |>
  calculate(stat = "diff in props", order = c("placebo", "vaccine"))
```

###

Our shuffle gave 2/6 - 9/14 = -0.310, one of the chapter's own examples. A difference due to chance alone can go either way, and this one favors the placebo.

### Exercise 3

Change the code so that it runs 100 shuffles, as the chapter does, and then counts how many shuffles gave each value of the difference. Render.

```{r}
#| label: simulating-the-study-3
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: simulating-the-study-3-test
#| echo: true
set.seed(19)
malaria |>
  specify(response = outcome, explanatory = treatment, success = "infection") |>
  hypothesize(null = "independence") |>
  generate(reps = 100, type = "permute") |>
  calculate(stat = "diff in props", order = c("placebo", "vaccine")) |>
  count(stat)
```

###

A hundred shuffles produced only six different values, because with 6 placebo patients the number infected can only be 0 through 6, giving seven possible differences in all. The observed 0.643, all six placebo patients infected, is the largest difference this study can produce.

### Exercise 4

Replace the count with the number of the 100 shuffles whose difference is at least as large as the observed one. Render.

```{r}
#| label: simulating-the-study-4
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: simulating-the-study-4-test
#| echo: true
set.seed(19)
malaria |>
  specify(response = outcome, explanatory = treatment, success = "infection") |>
  hypothesize(null = "independence") |>
  generate(reps = 100, type = "permute") |>
  calculate(stat = "diff in props", order = c("placebo", "vaccine")) |>
  summarize(at_least_observed = sum(stat >= 0.64))
```

###

Our 100 shuffles match the chapter's: two of the 100 simulations had a difference of at least 64.3%. The observed difference is 9/14 = 0.6428..., so a cutoff of `stat >= 0.643` would count zero shuffles.

### Exercise 5

Replace the code in that chunk so that it creates `null_dist`, the differences from 1,000 shuffles, with a seed set first. Print `null_dist`. Render.

```{r}
#| label: simulating-the-study-5
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: simulating-the-study-5-test
#| echo: true
set.seed(15)
null_dist <- malaria |>
  specify(response = outcome, explanatory = treatment, success = "infection") |>
  hypothesize(null = "independence") |>
  generate(reps = 1000, type = "permute") |>
  calculate(stat = "diff in props", order = c("placebo", "vaccine"))

null_dist
```

###

These 1,000 differences form a *randomization distribution*, which describes the shape, center, and variability of all possible values of a sample statistic from random allocations of the treatment variable. Each row is one rerun of the study's random assignment.

### Exercise 6

Start a new chunk that uses `null_dist` to calculate the mean of the simulated differences. Render.

```{r}
#| label: simulating-the-study-6
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: simulating-the-study-6-test
#| echo: true
null_dist |>
  summarize(mean_diff = mean(stat))
```

###

Our mean is 0.014, close to zero. The distribution of these simulated differences is centered around 0 because we simulated these differences assuming that the independence model was true.

### Exercise 7

Replace the code in that chunk so that it calculates, from `null_dist`, the proportion of shuffles with a difference at least as large as the observed 0.643. Use **infer**. Render.

```{r}
#| label: simulating-the-study-7
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: simulating-the-study-7-test
#| echo: true
obs_diff <- malaria |>
  specify(response = outcome, explanatory = treatment, success = "infection") |>
  calculate(stat = "diff in props", order = c("placebo", "vaccine"))

null_dist |>
  get_p_value(obs_stat = obs_diff, direction = "greater")
```

###

Our p-value is 0.012: 12 of 1,000 shuffles were as extreme as the study. Such a low probability indicates a rare event.

### Exercise 8

This study is small enough to skip simulation and count every possible random assignment. Replace the code in that chunk with a small table of three numbers: the number of ways to choose 6 placebo patients from 20, the number of those ways that put all 6 among the 11 who got an infection, and the second divided by the first. Render.

```{r}
#| label: simulating-the-study-8
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: simulating-the-study-8-test
#| echo: true
tibble(all_assignments = choose(20, 6),
       all_placebo_infected = choose(11, 6),
       proportion = all_placebo_infected / all_assignments)
```

###

Only 462 of the 38,760 possible assignments put all six placebo patients among the infected, a proportion of 0.0119, against our simulated 0.012. Usually it's not feasible to generate the full distribution of all possible values of the sample statistic, but 20 volunteers make it small enough to count.

### Exercise 9

Replace the code in that chunk with a bootstrap distribution: resample the 20 volunteers with replacement 1,000 times, with a seed set first, and calculate the same difference in infection rates for each resample. Show the mean of the 1,000 differences. Render.

```{r}
#| label: simulating-the-study-9
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: simulating-the-study-9-test
#| echo: true
set.seed(15)
malaria |>
  specify(response = outcome, explanatory = treatment, success = "infection") |>
  generate(reps = 1000, type = "bootstrap") |>
  calculate(stat = "diff in props", order = c("placebo", "vaccine")) |>
  summarize(mean_diff = mean(stat))
```

###

Our bootstrap mean is 0.652, near the observed 0.643, while the randomization distribution, which describes the null hypothesis, centered near 0. Since bootstrap distributions are generated by randomly resampling from the observed data, they are centered at the sample statistic.

### Exercise 10

Replace the code in that chunk with a bar plot of `null_dist`: the number of shuffles for each value of the difference, with the bars at least as large as the observed difference in a different color. Render.

```{r}
#| label: simulating-the-study-10
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: simulating-the-study-10-test
#| echo: true
null_dist |>
  ggplot(aes(x = stat, fill = stat >= 0.64)) +
  geom_bar()
```

###

The bars sit at six of the seven possible differences. The seventh, -0.786, which needs all six placebo patients free of infection, never came up.

### Exercise 11

Improve the plot. Make the bars narrower, use grey for the ordinary bars and a strong color for the extreme one, drop the legend, and add a title, axis labels, a subtitle that states the main finding, and a caption giving the number of volunteers, the number of shuffles, and the source. Render.

```{r}
#| label: simulating-the-study-11
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: simulating-the-study-11-test
#| echo: true
null_dist |>
  ggplot(aes(x = stat, fill = stat >= 0.64)) +
  geom_bar(width = 0.15) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("grey60", "firebrick"), guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "Differences in Infection Rates When the Vaccine Does Nothing",
       subtitle = "Only 12 of 1,000 shuffles matched the observed difference of 64.3 percentage points",
       x = "Difference in Infection Rates (Placebo Minus Vaccine)",
       y = "Number of Shuffles",
       caption = "20 volunteers, 1,000 shuffles under the independence model\nLyke et al. (2017), via openintro")
```

###

When we conduct formal studies, usually we reject the notion that we just happened to observe a rare event. So we conclude the data provide strong evidence that the vaccine provides some protection against malaria in this clinical setting.

Commit `analysis.qmd` with the message `"Simulate the malaria study"` and push.

7d42e90 (HEAD -> main, origin/main) Simulate the malaria study
3f8a1c2 Explore the malaria vaccine data

###

Errors do occur, just like rare events, and we might choose the wrong model. While we do not always choose correctly, statistical inference gives us tools to control and evaluate how often decision errors occur.

## Summary

This tutorial covered [Chapter 15: Applications: Foundations](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/foundations-applications.html) from [*Introduction to Modern Statistics*](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/) by Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel and Johanna Hardin. You have learned to judge whether a difference between two groups in a small randomized experiment could be due to chance alone, by simulating the experiment's random assignment many times, and to tell apart the data, randomization, and bootstrap distributions.

For the trial itself, read "[PfSPZ vaccine induces strain-transcending T cells and durable protection against heterologous controlled human malaria infection](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1615324114)" by Lyke and colleagues, the source the `malaria` help page cites. For more practice with these ideas, the chapter points to OpenIntro's [Tutorial 4: Foundations of inference](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims-tutorials/04-foundations/).

Many sentences in this tutorial come from the chapter, and its figure from [Chapter 2](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/data-design.html), all used under the book's [CC BY-SA 3.0 license](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/).

Your first plot is a data distribution and your second a randomization distribution. A distribution always describes variability, but sometimes it is worth reflecting on *what* is varying.
